# Step-5 CUDA performance validation

Unless stated otherwise, model measurements use the restored TypeSafeAI Q3_K_M checkpoint with 184 NeuroSenko BF16/F32 indexer tensors. They do not measure a newly converted official checkpoint or establish a broad quality score. The implementation and numerical contract are described in [step5.md](step5.md).

## Conditions

- Intel Core Ultra 7 265K, 20 inference and batch threads.
- Five 48 GiB Ada GPUs and one 24 GiB RTX 3090; CUDA 13, compute capabilities 8.9 and 8.6.
- `CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER=PCI_BUS_ID`, `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2,1,0,5,4,3` for every GPU test.
- Context 144000, allocated as 144128; batch 2048, microbatch 512, one server slot, F16 K/V, Flash Attention enabled, context shifting disabled.
- Eager CPU weight loading with `--load-mode none`; CPU expert offload and `--no-op-offload`; separate vision projector on CPU.
- Auto-fit with 2048 MiB device margin generated a placement; paired launches then fixed that placement with fitting disabled. The new indexed attention generated exactly the same fit plan as the earlier direct attention kernel.
- `-ngl 96`, tensor split `17,14,14,14,13,24`, plus the saved per-tensor CPU expert overrides. Target-only and MTP main-model buffers matched; MTP adds its three draft heads and small SWA cache.
- Greedy sampling, seed 1, full uncached prefill (`cache_prompt=false`), warmup with a 7382-token retrieval prompt. Retrieval-31K was run twice per comparison profile. Other long cases were single measurements.
- Fixed MTP comparisons use `--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3` and `LLAMA_MTP_ADAPTIVE=0`. Adaptive MTP is measured separately.

Complete local artifacts include requests, responses and output token IDs, server logs, sampled resources, exact arguments, environment, build options, binary SHA-256 hashes and source patches. Old binaries and all their shared libraries were isolated in a snapshot. Repeated launches do not run concurrently, and no other full model was loaded during measurements.

## Indexed attention

The former CSA attention kernel directly computed each selected query/head dot product and softmax with FP32 reductions. It was the dominant prefill operation. The new path maps each provider's logical token selection to physical cache rows and uses the existing indexed tensor-core Flash Attention machinery with 192-dimensional heads. Four providers become four independent attention streams with 16 query heads each. Negative row IDs represent causal or padded entries. Every nonnegative row ID must be below the physical cache capacity; the CSA slot map supplies those valid physical rows.

No full dense mask or duplicated K/V cache is built. Original K/V rows are read using the selected physical indices. Multi-token MTP verification uses the same path. Unusual shapes and separate physical sequence streams retain the direct kernel fallback. Independent logical sequences in one physical cache stream are supported by the row map.

The native CUDA implementation uses F16 probability and accumulator tiles. Its `GGML_PREC_F32` setting must not be interpreted as a promise of FP32 tensor-core accumulation. CPU indexed attention honors the explicit FP32 accumulator request. Floating-point comparisons account for this difference; index selection itself must agree exactly.

For isolated 512-query / 32768-history / 4104-selected-token operator checks, including summaries, scores, top-k, row mapping and attention:

| Device | Direct chain, median ms | Indexed chain, median ms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Logical CUDA0, Ada | 174.325 | 2.878 |
| Logical CUDA5, Ampere | 422.432 | 7.598 |

These are five measured repetitions after three warmups on synthetic inputs. They are not full-model speedups. On Ada, the profiled direct attention took about 173.53 ms. The indexed attention took about 2.214 ms; top-k 0.228 ms, score processing 0.220 ms, score GEMM 0.145 ms, summary compression 0.053 ms, row mapping 0.051 ms and copies 0.056 ms. Profiling and timing runs are separate.

## Full-model measurements

| Mode | PP, tokens/s, two runs | TG, tokens/s, two runs | Output tokens per run | Stop |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CSA direct, fixed MTP 3 | 63.71 / 63.64 | 12.66 / 12.46 | 93/93 | eos/eos |
| Legacy dense, fixed MTP 3 | 149.84 / 149.65 | 17.60 / 18.15 | 94/94 | eos/eos |
| Corrected dense, fixed MTP 3 | 151.65 / 152.41 | 18.53 / 18.59 | 88/88 | eos/eos |
| Corrected dense, no MTP | 155.21 / 155.30 | 14.80 / 14.92 | 96/96 | limit/limit |
| Indexed CSA, fixed MTP 3 | 152.80 / 152.58 | 16.87 / 17.14 | 91/91 | eos/eos |
| Indexed CSA, no MTP | 153.74 / 155.21 | 13.96 / 13.94 | 91/91 | eos/eos |

Every 31K run retrieved both facts. Corrected dense target-only reached its 96-token response limit; the other rows ended normally. The different output lengths and accepted draft counts matter when comparing TG.

| Mode, 59999 input tokens | PP, tokens/s | TG, tokens/s | Accepted / generated draft tokens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Legacy dense, fixed MTP 3 | 128.64 | 22.80 | 36 / 42 |
| Corrected dense, fixed MTP 3 | 128.38 | 21.54 | 35 / 45 |
| Indexed CSA, fixed MTP 3 | 132.76 | 24.15 | 37 / 39 |
| Indexed CSA, no MTP | 127.02 | 13.60 | none |

All 60K rows retrieved eight facts and produced 50 output tokens with normal end of response. Each row is one measured request.

| Mode, 142980 input tokens | PP, tokens/s | TG, tokens/s | Output tokens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Indexed CSA, no MTP | 133.68 | 12.35 | 50 |
| Indexed CSA, fixed MTP 3 | 131.53 | 21.34 | 50 |

Both 143K rows retrieved all eight facts, produced identical token IDs and ended normally. Dense modes were measured through 60K input with the same 144K allocation; no dense 143K speed is claimed.

The repeated 31K CSA prefill decreased from 487.05 / 487.55 seconds to 203.07 / 203.35 seconds, about 2.40x faster. Fixed-MTP TG changed from 12.66 / 12.46 to 16.87 / 17.14 tokens/s, with 93 versus 91 generated tokens.

Adaptive MTP on the same 31K prompt used a 256-token response budget and completed normally in 91 tokens: PP 152.75, TG 18.59 tokens/s, 49 / 73 accepted/generated draft tokens over 41 draft calls. Fixed MTP generated 108 draft tokens over 36 calls. The adaptive result differs from target-only by one synonymous word after 87 common token IDs; it is not a bit-exact match. This is one measurement, not a general adaptive-throughput claim.

Do not compare these 144K-allocation figures with older 64K-allocation measurements as though placement were identical. A larger KV/workspace reservation can move more experts to CPU even for a 31K request. TG also depends on the response length and accepted draft tokens; a short structured answer is not directly comparable to a longer explanation.

## Correctness after acceleration

The production build passed the independent oracle on CPU, Ada and Ampere, including shuffled cache slots, two sequences in a unified cache, long-position indexer RoPE and early queries at positions 0, 7 and 8 with a populated large cache. Selected indices matched exactly. Indexed main attention required NMSE below 1e-6 and the documented value-scaled F16 absolute bound. The early one-key case was checked separately.

Existing backend attention coverage passed 15 indexed cases and 12 dense 192-wide cases on each tested GPU architecture. Dense cases include token generation, multi-token verification and prefill with different GQA ratios. The maskless stream-stride fix also has a 512-dimensional multi-stream regression case.

Cache checks passed in separated and unified modes. Serialized state survived the round trip with all 23641724 bytes unchanged. F16 reduction order after cache compaction produced a maximum logit difference of about 0.0011284 and NMSE below 5.56e-6, with the same greedy token. The cache checker requires absolute error below 0.002 and NMSE below 1e-5; verification checks retain the tighter absolute 0.001 threshold and also require greedy agreement. All 12 rejection/acceptance cases passed in both cache modes. These bounds apply to the small deterministic model, not arbitrary full-model logits.

New fixed-MTP CSA and target-only token IDs matched on the tested 7K, 15K, two 31K repetitions, 60K and 143K requests. Adaptive MTP matched at 7K; its 31K result changes only "requested" to "required" near the end of the explanation. Both facts remain correct, all 91 tokens fit, and the response ends normally. Corrected dense also diverges between target-only and MTP after 51 common tokens; its target-only explanation reaches the 96-token output cap. These observations do not prove bit-exact full-model greedy behavior on arbitrary requests. CSA remains experimental. It is the current Step-5 default; dense attention is available through explicit selection.

Tool and vision integration checks used a required-tool round trip, a synthetic red square, OCR of rendered digits 483726, and a subsequent text request returning 56 with MTP active again. Both new CSA target-only and MTP launches passed. The accelerated target-only 143K run also passed two cached repeats (142979 cached tokens, one new token) and a follow-up (143029 cached tokens, 33 new prompt tokens). Earlier adaptive-MTP cache checks passed at 60K/143K; the byte-level and numerical cache tests were repeated on the accelerated build.

## Incremental region summaries

CSA now reuses unchanged eight-token region summaries between microbatches. Only regions affected by KV writes, removals or other cache edits are recomputed. The BF16/E4M3 arithmetic and provider selection budget are unchanged. This removes repeated compression of the old prefix; query-dependent score GEMMs, top-k selection and attention still grow with their input sizes.

The summary cache adds about 205.49 MiB across the 23 full-attention layers at 144128 allocated tokens. Auto-fit accounts for it, so compare performance with a fixed weight placement. Set `LLAMA_STEP5_CSA_SUMMARY_CACHE=0` for the previous uncached summary path. Separate physical sequence streams and single-sequence unified caches use this optimization; a multi-sequence unified cache retains the reference path.

CPU checks compared cached and uncached operations on F32/F16/BF16 synthetic K/Z, including 26000-token histories, cache hits, one-region changes and incomplete regions. Small-model F16/Q8_0 checks produced identical logits for append, speculative verification/rejection, prefix replacement across the 4096-token fast-path boundary, sequence copies and full/sequence state restores. Full-checkpoint CUDA prefill speedups are not established by these CPU checks.

## Region scoring and top-k (2026-10-18)

The persistent summary cache now uses F16 instead of F32. E4M3 summary values are exact in F16, so this changes neither their values nor the score formula. The cached summary operation emits F16 directly and score GEMM reads that output without a whole-summary conversion kernel. For a single physical stream, that output aliases the persistent cache, so cache hits also avoid copying the summary. Multiple physical streams use a separate contiguous output. The F32 reference path remains available. Scratch allocation omits the converted-summary array for F16 input.

CUDA selection uses four-bit radix histograms rather than 32 one-bit scans. Warp aggregation reduces histogram atomics on supported NVIDIA devices. Selection exits early if the remaining bucket is entirely selected. The final gather retains ascending region IDs and the existing lower-ID tie rule; the budget is still 512 regions. At this stage, score GEMM and provider reduction were separate operations. The subsequent fused path, now enabled by default for CSA prefill, is described below.

F16/F32 score and selected-index checks matched exactly on CPU, logical CUDA4 (Ada) and logical CUDA5 (Ampere). Top-k matched an independent stable-sort oracle in 55 synthetic cases on each of these backends, including signed zeros, infinities, tied scores, adjacent FP32 values and region counts through 131072. Small-model F16/Q8_0 cache lifecycle checks passed in six CPU configurations; CPU MTP checks also covered host/backend media inputs, 4233-token histories and three-head drafting. These numerical checks do not establish a full-checkpoint prefill speedup. Dedicated checkpoint measurements are recorded below.

A paired CUDA-event microbenchmark on logical CUDA4 used identical synthetic scores for both kernels, 512 queries, 512 selected regions, six alternating rounds and 30 kernel calls per timing sample. # Step-5 Preview

Step-5 uses the STEP35 GGUF architecture: 92 decoder layers and three appended MTP layers, hidden width 4096, 64 query heads, four KV heads, head width 192, and a repeating pattern of three 512-token sliding layers followed by one sparse layer. There are 352 routed experts and eight active experts per token.

The reference is [StepFun's standalone implementation](https://huggingface.co/stepfun-ai/Step-5-Preview/tree/364b3b03fed2477aa0953fe855a2c4c8c48ee3cc/inference), revision `364b3b03fed2477aa0953fe855a2c4c8c48ee3cc`. The original preview GGUF can be used with restored indexer tensors; matching dimensions does not establish identical weights to the official release.

## CUDA build and launch

Complete inference was developed and validated in a CUDA configuration with CPU expert offload and an optional CPU or CUDA projector. Full CPU-only execution and other GPU backends have not been validated. Numerical CPU operator coverage is separate from complete-model validation.


Keep all eight restored parts in the same directory. The original seven-part TypeSafeAI release lacks required indexer tensors. The validated Ampere/Ada build additionally used `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="86-real;89-real"`; use architectures that match the actual devices. `GGML_NATIVE=ON` targets the build machine's CPU.

The script uses context 144000, batch 2048, microbatch 512, F16 K/V, Flash Attention, eager CPU weight loading (`--load-mode none`), 20 CPU threads, one slot and disabled context shifting. It selects auto-fit with a 2048 MiB device margin and the requested minimum context. Context, batch, microbatch, threads and model/binary paths are configurable through `STEP5_CONTEXT`, `STEP5_BATCH`, `STEP5_UBATCH`, `STEP5_THREADS`, `STEP5_THREADS_BATCH`, `STEP5_MODEL` and `STEP5_SERVER`.

Set `STEP5_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0` to use Q8_0 for the main model K and V, including CSA. Draft K/V have separate options described below. The default remains `f16`. Direct CLI launches can use `--cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 -fa on`. CSA requires matching F16/F16 or Q8_0/Q8_0 caches; mixed formats and other cache types are rejected. Indexer K/Z remain canonical BF16. The CUDA indexed path dequantizes selected Q8_0 blocks into shared-memory tiles for the existing tensor-core attention kernel, without a full F16 copy of the KV cache. CPU fallback supports Q8_0; explicit FP32 indexed attention uses a dequantized K row and the original FP32 query. On Ampere and newer CUDA devices, the 192-wide Q8_0 indexed kernel preloads compressed tiles with `cp.async`: V loading overlaps Q x K, and the next K loading overlaps attention x V. A single compressed shared-memory buffer adds 6.5 or 13 KiB per block; there is no additional global cache copy. Devices without asynchronous-copy support retain synchronous reads. On Ada and Ampere, the independent numerical oracle, native indexed attention and small-model KV lifecycle checks passed. See [operator timing results](step5-performance.md#csa-q8_0-asynchronous-loading-2026-10-17) for the measured speedup; full-model throughput has not been compared for this loading change.

For one slot, context 131072, microbatch 512 and three MTP heads with matching main/draft cache types, cache tensor storage is about 11.89 GiB with F16 or 7.75 GiB with Q8_0 in CSA mode. This includes the key-only BF16 indexer cache and 186.88 MiB of derived region summaries, but excludes weights, projector, graph workspace and backend overhead. The indexer no longer allocates unused V tensors. Quantized K/V can change logits and generated text. Re-run auto-fit after changing the cache type; the numerical oracle is not a full-model quality benchmark.

CSA is the default for Step-5 in both the runtime and launcher; `LLAMA_STEP5_EXPERIMENTAL_CSA=1` is no longer required. Select corrected dense explicitly with `STEP5_ATTENTION=dense` in the launcher or `LLAMA_STEP5_EXPERIMENTAL_DENSE=1` for direct runtime launches. `STEP5_ATTENTION=legacy` selects the earlier dense scale/norm convention. The obsolete token-sparse experiment is not a launcher mode. Each mode sets its own runtime flags; explicit launcher mode selection clears conflicting inherited flags. Ordinary Step3.5 checkpoints keep their existing attention mode.

MTP defaults to three heads with existing adaptive draft length. Use `STEP5_MTP=0` for target-only execution, or `LLAMA_MTP_ADAPTIVE=0` for a fixed draft budget. The launcher passes `--spec-type` once, including when raw arguments override it. Functional MTP checks passed; adaptive decoding can change a synonymous word relative to target-only in the tested 31K explanation. The fixed-budget paired fixtures at microbatch 512 matched through 143K. These finite tests do not establish arbitrary-request bit-exact greedy behavior.

A separate Step-5 MTP GGUF can be selected with `--model-draft /path/to/Step-5-Preview-MTP-Q8_0.gguf --gpu-layers-draft all` appended to the launcher command. The loader accepts MTP-only files that retain all three heads, token embeddings, output norm and optional RoPE factors. Main-model MTP weights are skipped when an external draft is selected. The target still requires its CSA tensors. An MTP-only file is used as a draft, not as the target model.

The Q8_0 sidecar changes the 30 MTP matrices to Q8_0; its embeddings and norms are copied from the Q3 target for a controlled comparison with the extracted Q6_K sidecar. To select Q8_0 K/V for the draft as well, pass `--spec-draft-type-k q8_0 --spec-draft-type-v q8_0`. Weight quantization and KV cache type are independent.

For image requests, set `STEP5_MMPROJ=/path/to/mmproj-Step5-Preview-bf16.gguf`. The launcher adds `--no-mmproj-offload`, keeping the projector in RAM on CPU. Without a projector, use text/tool requests. Step-5 MTP accepts projected image embeddings and stays enabled when images remain in the conversation history. The projector still runs on CPU; MTP can accelerate text generation but does not accelerate image encoding.

For GPU vision, override the launcher with `--mmproj-device CUDA0`, or remove `--no-mmproj-offload` from a direct launch and select the desired logical CUDA device. Re-run auto-fit when changing the projector or its device. Projector memory planning includes the largest dummy-image compute buffers even with `--no-warmup`; that option still disables the runtime warmup. A compute-buffer allocation failure is returned as an image-processing error instead of continuing with an invalid graph. In the tested six-GPU Dense/Q8_0 configuration with vision on CUDA0, `--fit-target 1024,512,512,512,512,512` left about 965 MiB free on that device after image requests; a uniform 512 MiB margin left only 81 MiB.

The default address is `http://127.0.0.1:8085`, with the OpenAI-compatible API under `/v1`. `STEP5_HOST` and `STEP5_PORT` override it. Stop an existing server before starting another full copy. Prompt plus response must fit within the selected context. The largest checked initial prompt is 142980 tokens with microbatch 512; advertised 1M context and official-release weight identity remain unverified.

## Tensor compatibility

Each of the 23 full-attention layers requires these tensors. Dimensions below use GGML order.

| Source suffix under self_attn | GGUF suffix under blk.N | Dimensions | Convention |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| sparse_indexer_q.weight | indexer.q_proj.weight | 4096, 4096 | Raw BF16 |
| sparse_indexer_k.weight | indexer.k_proj.weight | 4096, 256 | Raw BF16 |
| sparse_indexer_z.weight | indexer.z_proj.weight | 4096, 256 | Raw BF16 |
| sparse_indexer_w.weight | indexer.proj.weight | 4096, 16 | Raw FP32 |
| sparse_indexer_q_norm.weight | indexer.q_norm.weight | 256 | Zero-centered RMSNorm: multiply by 1 + weight |
| sparse_indexer_k_norm.weight | indexer.k_norm.weight | 256 | LayerNorm scale, no offset |
| sparse_indexer_k_norm.bias | indexer.k_norm.bias | 256 | LayerNorm bias |
| ssmax_s | attn_ssmax_s | 64 | Preserve for checkpoint compatibility; unused by the reference |

The TypeSafeAI Q3_K_M model with the NeuroSenko restoration has eight splits, 1783 tensors, and all 184 required indexer tensors with the expected dimensions. Its main RMSNorm tensors already include the conversion offset. Restored indexer norms retain source values. Do not add the offset to both the stored tensor and the runtime expression.

The converter recognizes `Step5ForCausalLM`, `Step5ForConditionalGeneration`, and the earlier preview architecture names. Official model configs nest the text configuration under `text_config`.

## Reference attention

CSA compresses completed eight-token regions using a softmax over Z independently for each proxy coordinate. K is normalized and position-rotated first; Z is not normalized or rotated. Four provider groups each use four indexer query heads and select up to 512 historical regions, plus the query's current region. Main attention reads original token-level K/V with a causal mask.

Indexer RMSNorm is zero-centered; indexer LayerNorm uses the configured RMS epsilon. The reference keeps `ssmax_s` as an unused parameter and uses the usual inverse-square-root head scale for attention. Region-summary and score-input E4M3 rounding, and ties resolved by smaller logical region ID, are part of the reference contract.

The implementation below follows this contract. Token-level top-4096 selection is a separate legacy experiment and is not equivalent to regional CSA.

## Fused CSA score calculation

The combined CUDA score kernel is enabled by default for CSA prefill batches with at least 32 queries. Set `LLAMA_STEP5_CSA_FUSED_SCORES=0` before launch to use the previous cuBLAS path. Smaller decode/MTP batches keep the cuBLAS path in either mode. This changes neither the 512-region budget nor the attention mode.

On Ampere/Ada, the kernel uses the existing FP16 tensor-core primitives with FP32 accumulation. Each block processes 64 regions and eight queries. Per-head ReLU and the ordered weighted sum of four heads are applied before writing the four provider scores; the 16-head dot-product matrix is not written to global memory. Query E4M3 conversion stays separate. Both F16 and F32 summaries are accepted, and the CPU implementation keeps its reference score arithmetic.

With 144128 allocated tokens and microbatch 512, the score backing buffer, including scratch and allocation padding, decreases from 844.50 to 144.87 MiB. This is an operator-buffer calculation, not the reduction in total process VRAM. Auto-fit accounts for the smaller graph allocation; rerun fitting when changing the flag. Compare fixed placement first to separate the kernel change from moving more experts to GPU. On the tested IQ3_M checkpoint at 26K, fixed-placement prefill was unchanged; rerunning auto-fit moved 2.66 GiB more weights to GPU and improved mean prefill by about 9%. See [the performance report](step5-performance.md) for CUDA numerical checks and measurements.

## Numerical oracle

Use `--kv-type q8_0` with `examples/step5/check.py` to compare Q8_0 cache reads and attention against independently dequantized GGUF blocks. The default `--kv-type f16` retains the F16 fixtures. Both formats require exact agreement on selected token indices. Add `--fused-scores` to validate the compact score operation; this checker option also exercises short query batches that the runtime leaves on cuBLAS.

Run `python examples/step5/reference.py --output report.json --fixtures fixtures` in a Python environment with PyTorch and NumPy. This uses CPU calculations and does not load the model. It checks dense equivalence before the region budget is exceeded, causal selection, provider isolation, zero-centered norms and stable ties. Binary fixtures provide independent expected results for backend validation.

## Attention compatibility mode

Step-5 uses the reference attention scale by default. Set `LLAMA_STEP5_LEGACY_ATTENTION=1` to reproduce the previous `ssmax_s` scale and indexer normalization for a controlled dense comparison. This flag does not affect ordinary Step3.5 checkpoints. Indexer affine parameters, projections, normalization outputs and RoPE outputs are rounded to BF16 in the corrected path.

CPU normalization matched the independent PyTorch fixture exactly. CUDA on Ada and Ampere matched Q exactly; one of 32768 K values differed by one BF16 ULP (0.00390625), within the FP32 reduction tolerance. Existing GGML NORM, RMS_NORM and RoPE backend checks also passed on CUDA.

## Experimental grouped CSA

Step-5 enables region compression and four independent provider groups by default. `LLAMA_STEP5_EXPERIMENTAL_CSA=1` remains an explicit CSA selection and takes precedence over the dense and token-sparse flags; combining it with legacy attention is rejected. `LLAMA_STEP5_EXPERIMENTAL_DENSE=1` selects dense attention, and `LLAMA_STEP5_LEGACY_ATTENTION=1` selects legacy dense attention. The older `LLAMA_STEP5_EXPERIMENTAL_SPARSE=1` still selects individual tokens and is a separate comparison mode. A mode flag selects that mode only when its value is `1`; setting the CSA flag to `0` does not select Dense. CSA requires matching F16/F16 or Q8_0/Q8_0 K/V and Flash Attention. Keep context shifting disabled.

The indexer uses BF16 projection/norm/RoPE boundaries and E4M3 score inputs. Precise CUDA trigonometry preserves the BF16 reference table at long positions despite the build's global fast-math flags. The indexed prefill path combines top-k selection and physical row mapping for batches of at least 128 queries. Smaller decode and MTP batches retain separate selection and mapping. Both paths read original K/V through native indexed Flash Attention, including multi-token verification batches. It does not materialize the intermediate logical-token list; direct row mapping remains available for other selection inputs. Unusual layouts retain a direct attention kernel fallback. Independent logical sequences in a unified physical cache use the indexed path.

Run `python examples/step5/check.py --libdir build/bin --backend CUDA0 --output csa.json` with PyTorch and NumPy; `CPU` and other logical CUDA device numbers are also accepted. Checks cover the reference boundary lengths, signed head weights, stable ties, shuffled cache slots, independent sequences, and 192-wide attention with 64 query heads. Norm/RoPE fixtures at positions 0, 4096 and 143999 matched the official Triton kernel exactly on Ada and Ampere. Selected indices matched the independent oracle exactly in all fixtures. Rare FP32 summary reductions can straddle a BF16 midpoint before E4M3; the validator reports those elements and requires them to stay in the quantization interval of a 1e-6 FP32 error bound.

The accelerated path also covers queries at positions 0, 7 and 8 with a populated 8192-slot cache. Native CUDA Flash Attention uses F16 probability and accumulator tiles; it is not an FP32-accumulation promise. Indexed attention requires NMSE below 1e-6 and a value-scaled absolute bound; the one-key case is checked separately. CPU indexed attention honors the explicit FP32 accumulator request. Numerical operator checks and full-model checks are separate.

CUDA top-k uses four-bit radix histograms, at most eight rounds, with early exit when the remaining bucket is entirely selected. It retains the same region budget, ascending region IDs and lower-ID preference for equal scores. The fused path described above combines score GEMM and provider reduction for prefill by default. Setting `LLAMA_STEP5_CSA_FUSED_SCORES=0` or using fewer than 32 queries retains separate operations.

## Cache and memory

CSA stores canonical BF16 K/Z token projections in the indexer cache. Region summaries are cached per layer and physical sequence stream. Each KV write or removal changes the affected eight-token region's version; unchanged completed regions reuse the same BF16/E4M3 result. Rejected MTP tokens invalidate their regions, including edits made while the dense short-context fallback is active. Prefix copies, cache clearing and state restore also invalidate the affected derived data. Summaries are rebuilt from canonical K/Z after restore and are not serialized. The key-only indexer has a new cache layout marker: saved CSA states from builds that allocated indexer V tensors must be recreated. Current-build sequence and full-state restore remain supported. Future completed regions are excluded per query before selection.

Summary caching is enabled by default with CSA for separate sequence streams or a single unified sequence (including `--parallel 1`). Multiple independent sequences sharing one unified stream keep the uncached summary path. Set `LLAMA_STEP5_CSA_SUMMARY_CACHE=0` before launch to use the uncached reference for comparison. The cache adds 520 bytes per region per CSA layer: about 205.49 MiB total across 23 layers at 144128 allocated tokens. Auto-fit includes these persistent buffers. Query-dependent scores, top-k selection and attention still run on each microbatch. The persistent summaries use F16, which exactly represents their E4M3 values. CUDA GEMM reads the F16 summaries directly, avoiding a repeated F32-to-F16 conversion. For one physical stream, the result views the persistent cache and unchanged regions require no summary copy; multiple physical streams retain a contiguous gathered result. The uncached F32 summary API remains available for reference comparisons.

The logical slot map handles independent sequences and physical cache fragmentation. Chunked prefill may append to an existing cache. Context shifting remains unsupported. CSA scratch is part of the GGML graph allocation, including the cuBLAS score workspace, so auto-fit measures it. The actual logical range bounds normal execution; full-cache graph reservation still measures the context limit.

Generate the small test GGUF with `PYTHONPATH=gguf-py python examples/step5/make-small.py`. Build `examples/step5/check-cache.cpp` against libllama and run it with the GGUF path and either `0` (separate streams) or `1` (unified cache). It checks chunk sizes 128/256, prefix copy, independent sequences, verification rollback, state restore into a context with microbatch 512, and CUDA graph reuse. Both modes kept the same greedy token. All 23641724 serialized bytes matched exactly after restore. F16 reduction order after cache compaction produced a maximum logit difference of about 0.0011284 and NMSE below 5.56e-6. The checker requires absolute error below 0.002, NMSE below 1e-5 and the same greedy token. These are bounds for the deterministic four-layer fixture, not the full checkpoint.

The six-GPU auto-fit plan for context 144000 and microbatch 512 with a 2048 MiB margin was used for full-model checks through 142980 input tokens. Indexed attention generated exactly the same placement as the previous direct kernel. Saved main-model placement was fixed for target/MTP and attention-mode comparisons; memory planning and model quality were checked separately.

## MTP verification

The existing three-head MTP implementation is reused, including its adaptive draft length. No new draft model is needed. Use `--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3`; set `LLAMA_MTP_ADAPTIVE=0` for fixed-budget comparisons. Disable drafting with a separate `--spec-type none --spec-draft-n-max 0` launch. Pass `--spec-type` once: repeated options append types.

`check-cache.cpp MODEL 0 verify` and `check-cache.cpp MODEL 1 verify` check all 12 acceptance counts for verification batches of two, three and four tokens. Each crosses an eight-token region boundary. After rejection, a clean target context that never decoded the rejected tokens is the reference. Both cache modes passed, with equal greedy tokens and maximum absolute logit error below the explicit 0.001 verification threshold on the deterministic four-layer test model. The 0.001 tolerance covers batch-dependent arithmetic on this test model; it is not a bound for the full checkpoint.

The oracle and CPU/CUDA summaries also cover extreme Z values. Per-coordinate denominators use the reference clamp at 1e-20; an underflowing coordinate returns zero instead of NaN.

With the restored Q3_K_M weights, microbatch 512 and identical main-model placement, the accelerated CSA path produced identical target-only and fixed-MTP output token IDs for the tested 7382-, 15503-, 31028-, 59999- and 142980-token prompts. The 31K case was repeated twice in each mode and returned the same 91 tokens. This finite set does not establish bit-exact greedy behavior on arbitrary requests. Before indexed acceleration, the older direct kernel returned both 31K facts correctly but diverged in its explanation after 46 common tokens; that particular discrepancy is absent in the new fixed-MTP checks.

The accelerated adaptive-MTP run matched target-only at 7K. On the same 31028-token prompt, it completed in 91 tokens with both facts correct, but changed one word in the closing explanation ("requested" versus "required") after 87 common token IDs. Its 256-token output budget did not cut the response. It generated 73 draft tokens over 41 calls, versus 108 over 36 fixed-budget calls, confirming actual budget adaptation. Corrected dense also shows target-only/MTP differences on 31K, after 51 common tokens. Full-model bit-exact greedy behavior is not established. CSA remains experimental despite being the Step-5 default. Functional cache and fact checks passed. Changing the prefill microbatch also changes full-model greedy wording in the measured 1024 case; exact operator fixtures and byte-preserving state restore do not guarantee batch-independent full-model token IDs.

## Full-model quality checks

Validation used the existing restored TypeSafeAI Q3_K_M checkpoint, not a newly converted official checkpoint. Its eight GGUF splits contain 1783 tensors, including all 184 restored indexer tensors. Matching dimensions does not prove identity to StepFun's released weights or general long-context accuracy.

Complete inference was tested on CUDA 13 with five 48 GiB Ada GPUs and one 24 GiB RTX 3090, plus CPU expert offload. Every GPU test used `CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER=PCI_BUS_ID` and `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2,1,0,5,4,3`. Numerical CPU operator checks also passed. CPU-only complete-model inference and other GPU backends were not tested.

Long requests used context 144000 (allocated as 144128), batch 2048, microbatch 512, 20 CPU threads, F16 K/V, Flash Attention and disabled context shifting. Auto-fit generated placement with a 2048 MiB device margin; paired runs then fixed that placement. MTP uses the existing three draft heads; fixed and adaptive budgets are measured separately.

| Input tokens | Check | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7382 | Two archive facts | 2/2, identical target-only/fixed-MTP token IDs |
| 15503 | Eight archive facts | 8/8, identical target-only/fixed-MTP token IDs |
| 31028 | Two facts and requested explanation, two repetitions per mode | 2/2, all 91 token IDs equal with target-only/fixed MTP |
| 59999 | Mixed archive, eight distributed facts | 8/8, all 50 token IDs equal, normal end of response, no input truncation |
| 142980 | Mixed archive, eight distributed facts | 8/8, all 50 token IDs equal, normal end of response, no input truncation |
| 142980, cached, accelerated target | Repeated archive | 8/8; 142979 cached input tokens, one token processed again |
| Approximately 143K, accelerated target | Follow-up asking for THETA and ALPHA in reverse order | 2/2; 143029 cached tokens, 33 new prompt tokens |
| 59999, cached, accelerated fixed MTP, microbatch 1024/2048 | Repeated archive and follow-up | 8/8 and 2/2 in both configurations |
| 59999, cached, earlier adaptive MTP | Repeated archive and follow-up | 8/8 and 2/2; 59995 cached input tokens on repeat |
| 142980, cached, earlier adaptive MTP | Repeated archive and follow-up | 8/8 and 2/2; 142976 cached input tokens on repeat; follow-up retained 143076 tokens |

Mixed archives contain Russian prose, Python, JSON, tables, request logs and English documents. `examples/step5/check-server.py` generates them using the running server's tokenizer, saves complete requests and responses, rejects contradictory values, and optionally checks prefix reuse and a follow-up turn. For example, `python3 examples/step5/check-server.py --url http://127.0.0.1:8086 --tokens 60000 143000 --follow-up --output step5-quality`. Output budgets must fit within the selected context. Checks deliberately disable sampling for repeatability.

New accelerated target-only and fixed-MTP servers passed real required-tool round trips, including structured arguments, a tool-result message and the final answer 17. Both used string `tool_choice: "required"`. Named-object enforcement is not supported by this server path. Parallel tool calls and strict-schema reliability on arbitrary requests were not tested.

Image checks used the separate projector on CPU: synthetic red-square recognition and OCR of rendered digits 483726. A subsequent text-only request returned 56; MTP drafting resumed in the MTP launch. These fixtures do not cover natural-image accuracy, a GPU projector or video.

The IQ3_M-AntirezLike-AttnQ8_0-MTPQ6_K build also passed eight CUDA image-history requests with CSA, Q8_0 main K/V, a CPU BF16 projector, context 144000, microbatch 512 and the default adaptive three-head MTP budget. Text prefixes contained 4594 or 25996 tokens before the first image. Each history tested image recognition, a text follow-up retaining that image, a second image retaining the first, and a question about both. MTP stayed enabled in all requests, and follow-ups reused the cached prefix without target/draft consistency resets. These finite checks use two synthetic images; see [the performance report](step5-performance.md) for the saved counting-request measurements.

The maximum checked initial prompt was 142980 tokens; the earlier adaptive-MTP follow-up retained 143076 tokens. No 1M-context validation is claimed. Performance comparisons control warmup, placement and prompt-cache reuse separately; see [the CUDA performance report](step5-performance.md).

# Using multiple GPUs with llama.cpp

This guide explains how to run [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) across more than one GPU. It covers the split modes, the command-line flags that control them, the limitations you need to know about, and ready-to-use recipes for `llama-cli` and `llama-server`.

The CLI arguments listed here are the same for both tools - or most llama.cpp binaries for that matter.

---

## When you need multi-GPU

Reach for multi-GPU when one of these is true:

- **The model doesn't fit in a single GPU's VRAM.** By spreading the weights across two or more GPUs the whole model can stay on accelerators. Otherwise part of the model will need to be run off of the comparatively slower system RAM.
- **You want more throughput.** By distributing the computation across multiple GPUs, each individual GPU has to do less work. This can result in better prefill and/or token generation performance, depending on the split mode and interconnect speed vs. the speed of an individual GPU.

---

## The split modes

Set with `--split-mode` / `-sm`.

| Mode | What it does | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| `none` | Use a single GPU only. Pick which one with `--main-gpu`. | You explicitly want to confine the model to one GPU even though more are visible. |
| `layer` (**default**) | Pipeline parallelism. Each GPU holds a contiguous slice of layers. The KV cache for layer *l* lives on the GPU that owns layer *l*. | Default and most compatible multi-GPU choice. You want more memory than a single GPU provides and your priority is a fast prefill. Can tolerate slow interconnect speeds between GPUs. |
| `row` | **Deprecated.** Older row-split tensor-parallel path with comparatively poor performance. Splits only dense weights across GPUs. Superseded by `tensor` which should be universally superior if it can be used. | Avoid in new deployments. |
| `tensor` | **EXPERIMENTAL.** Tensor parallelism that splits both weights *and* KV across the participating GPUs via a "meta device" abstraction. | You want more memory than a single GPU provides and your priority is fast token generation. Prefill speeds approach pipeline parallel speeds for large, dense models and fast GPU interconnect speeds. Treat as experimental as the code is less mature than pipeline parallelism. Performance should be good for multiple NVIDIA GPUs using the CUDA backend, no guarantees otherwise. |

> Pipeline parallel (`layer`) vs. tensor parallel (`tensor`): pipeline-parallel runs different layers on different GPUs and processes tokens sequentially through the pipeline. This minimizes data transfers between GPUs but requires many tokens to scale well. Tensor-parallel splits each layer across GPUs and does multiple cross-GPU reductions per layer. This enables parallelizing any workload but is much more bottlenecked by the GPU interconnect speed. Pipeline-parallel maximizes batch throughput; tensor-parallel minimizes latency.

---

## Command-line arguments reference

| Short | Long | Value | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `-sm` | `--split-mode` | `none` \| `layer` \| `tensor` | `layer` | See modes above. |
| `-ts` | `--tensor-split` | comma-separated proportions, e.g. `3,1` | mode-dependent | How much of the model goes to each GPU. If omitted, `layer`/`row` use automatic splitting proportional to memory, while `tensor` splits tensor segments evenly. With `3,1` on two GPUs, GPU 0 gets 75 %, GPU 1 gets 25 %. The values follow the order in `--device`. |
| `-mg` | `--main-gpu` | integer device index | `0` | The single GPU used in `--split-mode none`. |
| `-ngl` | `--n-gpu-layers` / `--gpu-layers` | integer \| `auto` \| `all` | `auto` | Maximum number of layers to keep in VRAM. Use `999` or `all` to push everything possible to the GPUs. |
| `-dev` | `--device` | comma-separated device names, or `none` | auto | Restrict which devices llama.cpp may use. See `--list-devices` for names. |
| | `--list-devices` | - | - | Print the available devices and their memory. Run this first to learn the names you'd pass to `--device`. |
| `-fa` | `--flash-attn` | `on` \| `off` \| `auto` | `auto` | Required when using `--split-mode tensor` and/or quantized V cache. Supported (and therefore enabled by default) for most combinations of models and backends. |
| `-ctk` | `--cache-type-k` | `f32` \| `f16` \| `bf16` \| `q8_0` \| `q4_0` \| ... | `f16` | KV cache type for K. |
| `-ctv` | `--cache-type-v` | same as `-ctk` | `f16` | KV cache type for V. |
| `-fit` | `--fit` | `on` \| `off` | `on` | Auto-fit unset args to device memory. **Not supported with `tensor`. You may need to manually set the `--ctx-size` to make the model fit.**  |

As for any CUDA program, the environment variable `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` can be used to control which GPUs to use for the CUDA backend: if you set it, llama.cpp only sees the specified GPUs. Use `--device` for selecting GPUs from among those visible to llama.cpp, this works for any backend.

---

## Recipes

### 1. Default - pipeline parallel across all visible GPUs


Easiest configuration. KV cache spreads across the GPUs along with the layers. `--fit` (on by default) sizes things automatically.

### 2. Pipeline parallel with a custom split ratio


Useful when GPUs have different memory: GPU 0 (3 parts) and GPU 1 (1 part). Proportions are normalized so `-ts 3,1` is the same as e.g. `-ts 75,25`.

### 3. Single-GPU mode, picking a specific GPU


Use only the device listed as `CUDA1` when calling with `--list-devices`.

### 4. Tensor parallelism (experimental)


- `--flash-attn off` or (`--flash-attn auto` resolving to `off` when it isn't supported) is a hard error.
- KV cache types must be non-quantized: `f32`, `f16`, or `bf16`. Support for quantized KV cache is not implemented and trying to use it will result in an error.
- Mark this configuration as experimental in your tooling: validate output quality before deploying.
- `--split-mode tensor`is not implemented for all architectures. The following will fail with *"LLAMA_SPLIT_MODE_TENSOR not implemented for architecture '...'"*:

  - **MoE / hybrid:** Grok, MPT, OLMoE, DeepSeek2, GLM-DSA, Nemotron-H, Nemotron-H-MoE, Granite-Hybrid, LFM2-MoE, Minimax-M2, Mistral4, Kimi-Linear, Jamba, Falcon-H1
  - **State-space / RWKV-style:** Mamba, Mamba2 (and the hybrid Mamba-attention models above)
  - **Other:** PLAMO2, MiniCPM3, Gemma-3n, OLMo2, BitNet, T5

### 5. With NCCL

There's no runtime flag for NCCL - it's selected at build time (`-DGGML_CUDA_NCCL=ON`, this is the default). Note that NCCL is **not** automatically distributed with CUDA and you may need to install it manually - when in doubt check the CMake log to see whether or not it can find the package. When llama.cpp is compiled with NCCL support it uses it automatically for cross-GPU reductions in `tensor` mode. When NCCL is missing on a multi-GPU build, you'll see this one-time warning and performance will be lower:


When using the "ROCm" backend (which is the ggml CUDA code translated for AMD via HIP), the AMD equivalent RCCL can be used by compiling with `-DGGML_HIP_RCCL=ON`. Note that RCCL is by default *disabled* because (unlike NCCL) it was not universally beneficial during testing.
### 6. With CUDA peer-to-peer access (`GGML_CUDA_P2P`)

CUDA peer-to-peer (P2P) lets GPUs transfer data directly between each other instead of going through system memory, which generally improves multi-GPU performance. It is **opt-in** at runtime - set the environment variable `GGML_CUDA_P2P` to any value to enable it:


P2P requires driver support (usually restricted to workstation/datacenter GPUs) and **may cause crashes or corrupted outputs on some motherboards or BIOS configurations** (e.g. when IOMMU is enabled). If you see instability after enabling it, unset the variable.

---

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | How to fix |
|---|---|
| Startup error *"SPLIT_MODE_TENSOR requires flash_attn to be enabled"* | Add `-fa on` or remove `-fa off`. |
| Startup error *"simultaneous use of SPLIT_MODE_TENSOR and KV cache quantization not implemented"* | Use `-ctk f16 -ctv f16` (or `bf16`/`f32`) with `--split-mode tensor`. |
| Startup error *"LLAMA_SPLIT_MODE_TENSOR not implemented for architecture 'X'"* | Architecture not on the TENSOR allow-list. Use `--split-mode layer`. |
| Warning *"NCCL is unavailable, multi GPU performance will be suboptimal"* | llama.cpp wasn't built with NCCL. Either accept the lower performance or install NCCL and rebuild. |
| CUDA OOM at startup or during prefill in `--split-mode tensor` | Auto-fit is disabled in this mode, so reduce memory pressure yourself. In order from least to most disruptive: lower `--ctx-size` (`-c`) (KV cache is roughly proportional to `n_ctx`); for `llama-server`, lower `--parallel` (`-np`) (a slot KV cache is allocated per concurrent sequence); as a last resort, reduce `--n-gpu-layers` (`-ngl`) (the remaining layers run on CPU and inference will be much slower). |
| Performance is worse with multi-GPU than single-GPU | The performance is bottlenecked by GPU interconnect speed. For `--split-mode tensor`, verify that NCCL is being used. Try `--split-mode layer` (less communication than `tensor`). Increase GPU interconnect speed via more PCIe lanes or e.g. NVLink (if available). |
| GPU not used at all | `--n-gpu-layers` is `0` or too low - try explicitly setting `-ngl all`. Or you are accidentally hiding the GPUs via an environment variable like `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=-1`. Or your build doesn't include support for the relevant backend. |
| Crashes or corrupted outputs after setting `GGML_CUDA_P2P=1` | Some motherboards and BIOS settings (e.g. with IOMMU enabled) don't support CUDA peer-to-peer reliably. Unset `GGML_CUDA_P2P`. |

# Multimodal

llama.cpp supports multimodal input via `libmtmd`. Currently, there are 2 tools support this feature:
- [llama-cli](../tools/cli/README.md)
- [llama-server](../tools/server/README.md) via OpenAI-compatible `/chat/completions` API
- [llama-mtmd-cli](../tools/mtmd/README.md), for testing and development

Currently, we support **image**, **audio** and **video** input.

To enable it, you can use one of the 2 methods below:

- Use `-hf` option with a supported model (see a list of pre-quantized model below)
    - To load a model using `-hf` while disabling multimodal, use `--no-mmproj`
    - To load a model using `-hf` while using a custom mmproj file, use `--mmproj local_file.gguf`
- Use `-m model.gguf` option with `--mmproj file.gguf` to specify text and multimodal projector respectively

By default, multimodal projector will be offloaded to GPU. To disable this, add `--no-mmproj-offload`

## MiniCPM-V 4.6

### Prepare models and code

Download [MiniCPM-V-4_6](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/MiniCPM-V-4_6) PyTorch model from huggingface to "MiniCPM-V-4_6" folder.

The model must be the standard `transformers` v5.7.0+ checkpoint (no `trust_remote_code`); the architecture in `config.json` is `MiniCPMV4_6ForConditionalGeneration` with a `qwen3_5_text` text model and a SigLIP-based vision tower plus a window-attention `vit_merger`.

### Usage of MiniCPM-V 4.6

Unlike older MiniCPM-V variants, MiniCPM-V 4.6 is converted directly through `convert_hf_to_gguf.py`. The same script is invoked twice on the original Hugging Face directory: once to produce the language-model GGUF and once with `--mmproj` to produce the multimodal projector GGUF.

# llama.cpp INI Presets

## Introduction

The INI preset feature, introduced in [PR#17859](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/17859), allows users to create reusable and shareable parameter configurations for llama.cpp.

## Using Presets with the Server

When running multiple models on the server (router mode), INI preset files can be used to configure model-specific parameters. Please refer to the [server documentation](../tools/server/README.md) for more details.

### Using a Hugging Face Preset

> [!IMPORTANT]
>
> Please only use presets that you can trust! Unknown presets may be unsafe

You can push your preset to Hugging Face Hub and share with other users by:
1. Creating an empty model repository on Hugging Face
2. Creating a `preset.ini` file in the root directory of the repository

## System-level config

The system-level config, added in PR [#26118](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26118), allows sharing the same set of options among multiple tools and examples. Unlike the sections above, it is not limited to the server.

These files are loaded on startup if present. A later file overrides an earlier one:
1. System-wide: `/etc/llama.cpp/config.ini` (or `%PROGRAMDATA%\llama.cpp\config.ini` on Windows)
2. User-level: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/llama.cpp/config.ini`, `~/.config/llama.cpp/config.ini` by default (or `%APPDATA%\llama.cpp\config.ini` on Windows)

The config file is applied first, then its options are overridden by ENV variables, CLI arguments and model presets (in router mode).

Note:
- Only the `[*]` and default sections are used; options written before any section header belong to "default. Named sections are ignored
- Tool-specific options can be specified, but will be ignored (with a warning) if the example doesn't support it<br/>Example: if you specify `port = 1234`, only `llama-server` will use it, other examples will ignore it
- `model` or `hf-repo` are not recommended to be configured system-level, because it may introduce conflicts<br/>Example: a `hf-repo` in the config file still takes effect when you pass `-m` on the command line, so you may load a different model than expected

# Release process

llama.cpp uses [semantic versioning](https://semver.org) (`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`).

## Version bump guidelines

| Change type | Version component |
|---|---|
| Breaking change to the public C API (`include/llama.h`)         | `MAJOR` |
| Backward-compatible features, model support, or API addition    | `MINOR` |
| Bug fix with no API change                                      | `PATCH` |

The version is set in the three variables at the top of the root `CMakeLists.txt`:


_A version bump should be included in the PR that introduces the change, or in a
dedicated bump commit merged before the release is cut._

_TODO: add PR labels (`semver: patch`, `semver: minor`, `semver: major`) to help
identify which PRs require a version bump before cutting a release._

## Making a release

Releases are created by running the [make-release](.github/workflows/make-release.yml)
which is a manual workflow.

The workflow runs against the branch selected in the "Run workflow" dialog
(default `master`) and takes an optional `commit` SHA. When a commit is given,
the workflow validates that the commit belongs to the branch and is not older
than 3 days from the branch HEAD, then releases that commit instead of the
branch HEAD.

The workflow creates an annotated git tag (e.g. `v0.1.0`) and pushes it to the
remote. No GitHub Release object is created, the tag is the release artifact.

## Building a release

By default, `LLAMA_BUILD_IS_DEV=ON` which appends a `-dev` suffix to `LLAMA_VERSION`,
marking the build as a nightly/development build. Distributors building from a
release tag must pass `-DLLAMA_BUILD_IS_DEV=OFF` to produce a clean version string
(e.g. `0.1.0` instead of `0.1.0-dev`).

## How releases reach users
Currently releases are not published to github releases, only nightly/development
builds are available there. The way users can access releases are using the following
channels:

- **llama-install.sh**  — downloads pre-built binaries built from the release tag.
- **Package managers**  — consume the git tag directly.
- **Build from source** — users clone the repo and check out the tag.

# Speculative Decoding

llama.cpp supports speculative decoding, a technique that can significantly accelerate token generation by predicting multiple tokens ahead of the main model.

[Speculative decoding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer_(deep_learning)#Speculative_decoding) leverages the fact that computing n tokens in a batch (as in prompt processing) is more efficient than computing n sequentially (as in response generation). By generating draft tokens quickly and then verifying them with the target model in a single batch, this approach can achieve substantial speedups when the draft predictions are frequently correct.

## Implementations

The `llama-server` application supports several implementations of speculative decoding. An implementation with draft model can be mixed with an implementation without draft model.

### Draft Model (`draft`)

A much smaller model (called the _draft model_) generates drafts.
A draft model is the most used approach in speculative decoding.

### EAGLE-3 (`draft-eagle3`)

EAGLE-3 uses a small draft model that reads the target model's hidden states to predict the next tokens, so it
reaches higher acceptance than a standalone draft model of the same size. The draft is a one-layer transformer
trained for a specific target model; it shares the target model's tokenizer and, optionally, uses a reduced draft
vocabulary with its own `lm_head`, which is mapped back using a `d2t` table.

Convert the EAGLE-3 checkpoint with `--target-model-dir` so it inherits the target's tokenizer and the layer
indices to read. Both the SpecForge `LlamaForCausalLMEagle3` and the vLLM/AngelSlim `Eagle3LlamaForCausalLM`
checkpoint formats are supported (for example [`AngelSlim/Qwen3-4B_eagle3`](https://huggingface.co/AngelSlim/Qwen3-4B_eagle3)
for `Qwen/Qwen3-4B`):


Supported EAGLE-3 draft models include:

- [yuhuili/EAGLE3-LLaMA3.1-Instruct-8B](https://huggingface.co/yuhuili/EAGLE3-LLaMA3.1-Instruct-8B)

For the full and up-to-date list of supported models, see #18039.

### DFlash (`draft-dflash`)

DFlash produces an entire block of draft tokens in a single forward pass (block diffusion) and
injects the target model's hidden states into the draft model's attention, instead of drafting one
token at a time. This keeps the draft model small while making drafting GPU-friendly. Unlike EAGLE-3
(a single-layer autoregressive draft), the DFlash draft uses several transformer layers but emits a
whole block per draft step.

The draft is a small block-diffusion model trained for a specific target (for example
`z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash` for `Qwen/Qwen3-4B`). Convert it with `--target-model-dir` so it inherits the
target's tokenizer and token embeddings:


`--spec-draft-n-max` is clamped to the draft model's trained block size.

See:

- #22105

### DSpark (`draft-dspark`)

DSpark extends DFlash with a semi-autoregressive _Markov head_: the draft still emits a whole
block per forward pass, but each block position's logits are biased by a low-rank term keyed on
the previous token, chained in-graph across the block. This keeps drafting at one decode per
block while recovering some of the left-to-right signal that pure block diffusion loses.

The draft is a small DeepSpec checkpoint trained for a specific target (for example
[`deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7`](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7)
for `Qwen/Qwen3-4B`). Convert it with `--target-model-dir` so it inherits the target's tokenizer
and token embeddings:


`--spec-draft-n-max` is clamped to the draft model's trained block size.

`--spec-draft-conf-min P` truncates each drafted block at the first position whose predicted
acceptance (from the draft's confidence head, if present) falls below `P` (default 0 = disabled).

Currently only drafts with a Qwen3 backbone are supported; support for other backbones
(e.g. Gemma4) is planned.

DSpark drafts exported in the [speculators](https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators) format
(for example [`RedHatAI/gemma-4-31B-it-speculator.dspark`](https://huggingface.co/RedHatAI/gemma-4-31B-it-speculator.dspark))
convert the same way.

See:

- #25173

### n-gram Cache (`ngram-cache`)

An n-gram is a sequence of n tokens. The n-gram cache implementation maintains statistics about short n-gram sequences.
A draft is computed using probabilities derived from these statistics. External statistics can also be loaded from files for improved accuracy.

See:

- #5479, #6828, #6848

### n-gram Map (`ngram-simple`, `ngram-map-*`)

These implementations search the token history for patterns and use matching sequences as draft candidates.
They require no additional model but rely on patterns that have already appeared in the generated text.
An example to use this approach can be the rewriting of source code by a LLM.

#### n-gram Map (`ngram-simple`)

This implementation looks for the last n-gram in history that matches the current n-gram and creates a draft using the m tokens following the matched n-gram. It is the simplest self-speculative approach with minimal overhead.


#### n-gram Map Key (`ngram-map-k`)

This implementation looks for the current n-gram of size n (called the _key_) in the token history. If the key n-gram is followed by the same m tokens (called the _mgram_) multiple times, it creates a draft using these m tokens. This approach requires a minimum number of occurrences (argument `--spec-ngram-map-k-min-hits`, default is 1) before generating drafts.

The number of accepted tokens is stored for each used n-gram.

**Example:**

#### n-gram Map Key-4-Values (`ngram-map-k4v`)

This experimental implementation looks for the current n-gram of size n (called the _key_) in the token history. For each key, up to four _values_ (n-grams of size m, called _mgrams_) are tracked. An internal statistic counts the occurrences of each mgram after the key n-gram. If one mgram is significantly more frequent than the others, it is used as the draft.

The number of accepted tokens is stored for each used n-gram.

**Example:** Server options to be used if there are a lot of longer repetitions.

### n-gram Mod (`ngram-mod`)

Add basic ngram hasher for speculative decoding:

- For each ngram, compute a hash using LCG
- For each computed hash, store the next token
- During speculation, iteratively compute the rolling hash of the last n tokens and pick the next token from the storage

Some characteristics:

- Lightweight (~16 MB)
- Constant memory and complexity
- Can generate variable draft lengths (i.e. m is not fixed)

Currently, a single hash pool is shared across all server slots, so different requests can benefit from each other.

**Sample usage:**


Applications:

- Iterating over a block of text/code (e.g. in llama.vim)
- Reasoning models (when they have to repeat their thinking in the final answer)
- Summarization

Example Video:

- See #19164

### Differences between ngram-simple, ngram-map and ngram-mod

- ngram-simple looks for a previous matching n-gram and inserts the following m-gram.
- ngram-map-k looks for a previous matching n-gram and inserts the following m-gram but uses an internal hash-map of n-grams in the current context window.
- ngram-mod uses a hash pool which is shared across all server slots. The hash pool is a map from n-gram hash to the next token (not the next m-gram as in ngram-map).

## Command-Line Options

If a draft model is combined with a draftless decoding the draftless decoding has higher precedence.

### Backend Sampling

Use `--backend-sampling` to run supported target-model samplers on the model backend. Draft-model sampling uses the backend by default and can be controlled with `--spec-draft-backend-sampling` and `--no-spec-draft-backend-sampling`.

Unsupported samplers and device layouts fall back to CPU sampling. Tensor split mode does not support backend sampling. A fixed seed produces repeatable random draws, but stochastic CPU and backend sampling can still select different tokens because floating-point operations can differ between implementations and devices. Use greedy sampling when exact output matching is required.

### Synthetic Acceptance

`llama-server` and `llama-cli` can replace normal speculative verification with synthetic decisions for benchmarking. The generated output is not valid model output because accepted draft tokens do not have to match the target model.

Use exactly one of these options:

- `--spec-synth-rates P0,P1,...` sets unconditional per-position acceptance probabilities. Entry `i` is the probability that the first `i+1` draft tokens are all accepted. The number of entries must match the effective maximum draft length. Values must be finite, within `[0, 1]`, and monotonically non-increasing.
- `--spec-synth-len L` sets the target mean acceptance length, including the target token. For `K` maximum draft tokens, `L` must be within `[1, K+1]`. The server finds a constant conditional probability `p` such that `p + p^2 + ... + p^K = L - 1`, then uses unconditional rates `[p, p^2, ..., p^K]`.

### `--spec-type TYPE`

Specifies a comma-separated list of speculative decoding types to use.

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `none` | No speculative decoding (default) |
| `draft-simple` | Use a simple draft model for speculation |
| `draft-eagle3` | Use an EAGLE-3 draft model that reads the target's hidden states |
| `draft-dflash` | Use a DFlash block-diffusion draft model that emits a block per step |
| `draft-dspark` | Use a DSpark draft model (DFlash backbone + semi-autoregressive Markov head) |
| `draft-mtp` | Use Multi Token Prediction (MTP) heads from the main model |
| `ngram-cache` | Use n-gram cache lookup |
| `ngram-simple` | Use simple n-gram pattern matching |
| `ngram-map-k` | Use n-gram pattern matching with n-gram-keys |
| `ngram-map-k4v` | Use n-gram pattern matching with n-gram-keys and up to four m-gram values (experimental) |
| `ngram-mod` | Use basic ngram hasher for speculative decoding with shared pool |

**Example:** Server-instance used to refactor source code.

**Example:** Multiple speculative implementations.

### `--spec-ngram-*-size-n N`

Sets the size N of the lookup n-gram for n-gram map based speculative decoding.
The n-gram size N determines how many tokens in a row to look back when searching for matching patterns.

Each n-gram implementation has its own parameter:

- `--spec-ngram-simple-size-n` for `ngram-simple`
- `--spec-ngram-map-k-size-n` for `ngram-map-k`
- `--spec-ngram-map-k4v-size-n` for `ngram-map-k4v`
- `--spec-ngram-mod-n-match` for `ngram-mod`

### `--spec-ngram-*-size-m M`

Sets the size M of the draft m-gram for n-gram map based speculative decoding.
The m-gram size determines how many tokens to draft when a match is found.
Larger values can provide more speedup but may reduce acceptance rate.

Each n-gram implementation has its own parameter:

- `--spec-ngram-simple-size-m` for `ngram-simple`
- `--spec-ngram-map-k-size-m` for `ngram-map-k`
- `--spec-ngram-map-k4v-size-m` for `ngram-map-k4v`

### `--spec-ngram-*-min-hits H`

This option defines how often a key has to appear in the token history to be used as a draft (default is 1).

Each n-gram implementation has its own parameter:

- `--spec-ngram-simple-min-hits` for `ngram-simple`
- `--spec-ngram-map-k-min-hits` for `ngram-map-k`
- `--spec-ngram-map-k4v-min-hits` for `ngram-map-k4v`

## Statistics
Each speculative decoding implementation prints statistics.





- `#calls(b,g,a)`: number of calls of begin (new prompt), generation and accumulation of this implementations
- `#gen drafts`: number of drafts generated by this implementation
- `#acc drafts`: number of drafts accepted (partially) by the main model
- `#gen tokens`: number of tokens generated by this implementation (including rejected tokens)
- `#acc tokens`: number of tokens accepted by the main model
- `dur(b,g,a): durations of begin (new prompt), generation and accumulation (process acceptance).

## Benchmarking

To measure the end-to-end effect of speculative decoding (throughput, latency, and draft acceptance) across diverse prompts, see the SPEED-Bench client in [tools/server/bench/speed-bench](../tools/server/bench/speed-bench/README.md).
It runs against a running `llama-server` and can compare a baseline run against a speculative-decoding run.
